title: Forge 1
section: Lesson 2: Measures of Location and Variability
text:
Lesson 2: Measures of Location and Variability
Devore 1.3, 1.4, and S2.

Ways to Frame the Discussion










  what you saw minus what you expected   how much it naturally varies L2 builds both halves   how surprising is that? a probability, under an assumed model L3 and L4 turn it into a number L8 to L13 supply the model. L18 applies it to a statistic. L21 onward runs this sentence again and again.




Let Them Invent the Vocabulary


Where it sits. Mean, median, trimmed mean. Three answers to one question. Which you report depends on what the tail is doing.


How wide it is. Standard deviation, variance, fourth spread. Same idea. Pair the mean with \(s\), pair the median with the fourth spread, and do not mix them.


Crazy observations. Fence them with the fourth spread, mild past \(1.5 f_s\) outside the fourths, extreme past \(3 f_s\). Say out loud that a committee picked 1.5. Then answer the question they will ask. Throwing one out is an ethics call, and it is no unless you can name the reason: a transcription error, a stopwatch that failed, a soldier who never ran the lane. “It weakens my conclusion” is not a reason.

title: Forge 1
text:
Lesson 4: Probability Basics
Devore 2.2.
The three axioms. Everything else in the block is derived from these, so derive them live rather than handing out a rule sheet.


\(P(A) \ge 0\) for every event \(A\).


\(P(S) = 1\).


For disjoint events, probability adds. \(P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \cdots) = \sum_i P(A_i)\) when no two of them can happen together.



    P(A1 ∪ A2 ∪ A3) =     P(A1) +     P(A2) +     P(A3)

The addition rule. The overlap is inside both circles, so adding \(P(A)\) and \(P(B)\) counts it twice. Subtract it once.

     P(A ∪ B) =     P(A) +     P(B) −     P(A ∩ B)

\[P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\]
Three events. Same idea run twice. Add the singles, subtract the pairs, add the middle back, because subtracting all three pairs takes the centre out one time too many.

   A B C + + + − − − +

\[P(A \cup B \cup C) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) - P(A \cap B) - P(A \cap C) - P(B \cap C) + P(A \cap B \cap C)\]
The complement rule. Same axiom. \(A\) and \(A^c\) are disjoint and union to \(S\), so their probabilities add to 1. Derive it live, do not hand it out.

    P(A) +    P(Ac) =    1

\[P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)\]

title: Comments on FDW 2026 and Workshop Week Drafts
text:
FDW 2026:

The five-week progression from immersion to readiness to practice teaching gives new faculty a clear path.
The teaching dimensions provide a shared understanding of what we do, why we do it, and our goals as instructors.
The June certification is a smart way to pressure-test the structure before new faculty arrive.

Workshop Week:

Course stratification by size with scaled expectations makes sense – large courses need more structure than small ones.
Writing down PD/CD roles and responsibilities clarifies expectations.
I would recommend against having outgoing CDs or APDs run a “best of” teaching lab during the transition. If the goal of this new structure is to make change - we’ve been asking the old leadership to make change for several semesters now.

title: Comments on FDW 2026 and Workshop Week Drafts
section: 3.1 Summative assessments built before the semester starts
text:
3.1 Summative assessments built before the semester starts

I will have all versions of all summative assessments (WPR 1 and WPR 2 and TEE) complete by the end of the summer.
The course project will be finalized as well.
Each assessment will include a rubric and a document mapping every question back to a student learning objective (SLO).
The goal is transparency - instructors will know from day one what expectations we have of students. We’ll walk a fine line between not teaching to the test and ensuring every instructor understands what to emphasize and what cadets will need to demonstrate on exams.

title: Comments on FDW 2026 and Workshop Week Drafts
section: 3.2 Teaching Labs (Forges) led by the APD
text:
3.2 Teaching Labs (Forges) led by the APD

I will run the teaching labs. With this much new material in 206, I think this is especially important.
Early on, I will personally lead both the expectations and demonstration portions of each teaching lab. I intend to do this for an extended period – not because others can’t, but because I want to set the standard and demonstrate it week in and week out. When I eventually ask others to lead specific portions, the intent and expectations will be clear because they’ve seen it modeled consistently.
Each teaching lab will focus on the next three lessons: the finer points of what we want cadets to know, what they’ll need to show on assessments, and the deeper understanding of the material so that instructors can teach at a deeper level – not just cover content, but teach it well.

title: Comments on FDW 2026 and Workshop Week Drafts
text:
3.3 Course Director responsibilities
The CD will own day-to-day course execution, including:

WebAssign management
Managing the Canvas page
Tracking course coverage to ensure sections stay aligned on pace and content
Maintaining the course schedule and syllabus
Coordinating make-up exams and enforcing late policies
Serving as the first line of support for instructor questions on content and grading
Providing regular course status updates to the PD - pace, emerging issues, and grade trends

title: Comments on FDW 2026 and Workshop Week Drafts
text:
3.4 Weekly team teaching meetings

I want to establish weekly team teaching meetings, and I expect the format will evolve as guidance crystallizes.
Attendance groupings will be determined by a mix of instructor seniority, experience, and off-hour availability.
The purpose: share ideas on what to teach and with demonstration for the next three lessons. Leadership will rotate among instructors, and I will track that rotation.
The intent is to build a culture where instructors learn from each other and take ownership of how they teach - not just what they teach.

Using AI
Give cadets a prompt to start from.

Can you help me with this problem? I’ll give you my answers and I want you to figure out what I did wrong. If I’m stuck, give me small hints to move me along. Don’t give me the right answer until I get it myself, then help me validate my understanding.



Emphasize
Hit these in class.


Categorical versus numerical, and within numerical, discrete versus continuous. Rounds fired on a range day is numerical and discrete. Time to finish a ruck is numerical and continuous. Branch is categorical.


Parameter versus statistic, and the population it came from versus the sample. The average ACFT score of the cadets you sampled is a statistic. The average across the whole Corps is the parameter you will never see.


Observational study versus designed experiment. Random assignment is the tell. Assigning squads at random to two training plans is an experiment. Comparing squads that already picked their own plan is observational.


Skew, from summary statistics and from a density curve. Mean above median is right-skewed, below is left-skewed, equal is symmetric. Same idea on a curve: the tail names the direction, not the tall side. A few very long repair times pull the mean above the median, so the distribution is right-skewed. A density that climbs across its support piles the area on the right, so the long tail runs left. That is left skew even though the picture goes up.

Lesson 5: Counting
Devore 2.3.
Every counting problem in 2.3 is one of four cells. Drawing \(k\) objects from \(n\) distinct objects, the only two questions are whether order matters and whether an object can be drawn twice.

Counting \(k\) draws from \(n\) objects, Devore notation








Without replacement
With replacement




Ordered
\(P_{k,n} = \dfrac{n!}{(n-k)!}\)
\(n^{k}\)


Unordered
\(C_{k,n} = \dbinom{n}{k} = \dfrac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}\)
\(\dbinom{n+k-1}{k}\)



With \(n = 10\) and \(k = 3\): 720 ordered without replacement, 1000 ordered with replacement, 120 unordered without replacement, 220 unordered with replacement.
Devore teaches only three of the four. Section 2.3 gives the product rule (\(n^{k}\)), \(P_{k,n}\), and \(C_{k,n}\). Unordered with replacement is not in the text and is not on any graded event, so it is there to complete the picture, not to assign.
